proposedDescription: Border privet is a spreading, many-stemmed shrub often planted as a hedge. Small oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, and narrow clusters of white flowers are followed by black fruits that can persist into the colder months. Its branches spread broadly, giving an untrimmed plant a loose, layered shape. The leaves may turn reddish-purple in autumn, with some retained in mild conditions. This Asian shrub has escaped cultivation in Connecticut, where it can establish in lightly managed areas.
identification: Look for opposite, smooth-edged oval leaves, narrow white flower clusters and small black fruits. Other privets are similar, so include young twigs and flowers in identification photographs.
actions: Check local invasive-plant guidance before planting. Confirm escaped shrubs and contain fruiting material during any locally recommended removal.
researchNotes: UConn text is by Mark Brand; Cornell supplies a separate character treatment but reuses Mehrhoff/UConn photographs, so those photographs are not independent evidence. Native European claim in an older NH guide was rejected as conflicting.

sources.title: Cornell Turfgrass and Landscape Weed ID: Border privet

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Mark H. Brand / University of Connecticut
claims: Spreading multistem shrub, opposite leaves, white panicles, black fruit, autumn color and Connecticut escape tendency.
Perennial shrub; entire opposite oval leaves; terminal white inflorescences.

proposedDescription: Boston ivy is a deciduous woody vine from eastern Asia, familiar on walls and other vertical surfaces. Branched tendrils end in adhesive pads that anchor the stems firmly. Mature leaves are usually broad and three-lobed, turning red or burgundy in autumn; young growth can carry three separate leaflets. Small blue-black fruits, often on red stalks, attract birds. Although commonly cultivated, it also grows outside gardens in disturbed places and on rocky ledges in parts of New England.
identification: Look for tendrils with adhesive discs, mostly three-lobed glossy leaves and blue-black berries on reddish stalks. Juvenile leaves can have three leaflets.
actions: Keep vines away from vulnerable wood, shingles and gutters and prevent them from overtopping trees. Check local planting guidance and document escapes separately from planted vines.
researchNotes: NCSU and Native Plant Trust are independently authored; juvenile leaf variation retained rather than an absolute simple-leaf claim. Not Hedera helix despite shared ivy common name.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension / Elisabeth Meyer identification course
claims: Deciduous vine, adhesive tendrils, leaf variation, fall color, berries and building/tree precautions.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: Bird-attracting blue fruit on red stalks; regional disturbed/rocky habitats and identification comparison.

proposedDescription: Bouncingbet, also called soapwort, is an upright perennial with smooth stems and opposite, lance-shaped leaves marked by several strong veins. Clusters of pale pink or white flowers bloom at the stem tips. Each flower usually has five slightly notched petals emerging from a long, narrow green or reddish tube; double-flowered garden forms also occur. Originally from Eurasia, it was widely cultivated. Its soapwort name recalls the saponins in the leaves, which were formerly used to make a washing liquid.
identification: Check opposite leaves with three to five strong veins, smooth stems and pink-white flowers backed by a long tubular calyx. Double garden forms may obscure the normal petal count.
actions: Keep unwanted garden spread contained and confirm plants before removal. Do not treat historical soap use as evidence that the plant is edible.
researchNotes: NCSU supplies morphology; Native Plant Trust independently supports Eurasian origin, cultivation and soap-use history. No medicinal efficacy or safe ingestion claim.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
claims: Perennial habit, opposite ribbed leaves, smooth stems and notched petals with tubular calyx.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: Eurasian introduction, cultivation, double flowers and historical saponin-based washing use.

proposedDescription: Box tree moth is an Asian moth whose caterpillars feed on boxwood. The larvae are green with black heads and contrasting dark and pale lengthwise stripes. They tie foliage with silk, leaving webbing, droppings and chewed leaves inside the shrub. Heavy feeding can strip the leaves and damage bark. Adults usually have white wings bordered broadly in dark brown, though a darker form also occurs. Hidden caterpillars among dense foliage make careful inspection of the plant's interior useful.
identification: Inspect boxwood for striped green caterpillars with black heads, silk and chewed leaves. Adult white-and-brown wings are suggestive, but similar moths require confirmation.
actions: Photograph suspected insects and damage and report them through your state plant-health service. Avoid moving suspect boxwood plants or clippings until you receive guidance.
researchNotes: CFIA and USDA APHIS provide separate national treatments. Current quarantine maps are linked through APHIS rather than frozen into profile prose; generations and timing vary by region.

sources.title: CFIA: Box tree moth fact sheet

claims: Larval stripes, black head, webbing and defoliation; adult pale and dark forms.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
claims: Boxwood pest recognition, reporting and movement-prevention guidance.

proposedDescription: Boxwood leafminer is a tiny fly whose young live and feed inside boxwood leaves. Infested leaves develop yellowish spots and swollen, blisterlike mines that later turn brown; heavy attacks can thin a shrub as damaged leaves fall early. The orange to reddish adults resemble small gnats and appear around boxwoods in spring. Several larvae may share one leaf. Because the insects are concealed between the leaf surfaces, checking the leaves themselves is more useful than looking only for flying adults.
identification: Look for blistered or discolored boxwood leaves containing pale larvae; empty pupal skins may project from leaf undersides after adult emergence.
actions: Have the damage confirmed before treatment. Monitor affected shrubs and consider locally recommended resistant boxwood selections when replacing plants.
researchNotes: Kaur/Dale UF account and Illinois Extension are independent syntheses. Sources differ on exact overwintering stage, so seasonal development is kept broad and no calendar date generalized.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Balwinder Kaur and Adam Dale / University of Florida IFAS
claims: Orange gnatlike adults, leaf-contained larvae, emergence windows and Buxus hosts.
Leaf spots/mines, premature leaf fall, multiple larvae per mine and resistant plant selections.

proposedDescription: Branched centaury is a small annual with delicate pink flowers above pairs of oval leaves. It often branches near the base and may stay only a few inches tall. Unlike some other centauries, it does not form a lasting rosette of leaves at ground level. Its tiny flowers have short stalks and a narrow tube that opens into spreading lobes. Native across parts of Europe, Asia and northern Africa, it occurs in North American fields and other disturbed ground as an introduced plant.
identification: Look for a small branching annual, opposite leaves, pink stalked flowers and no basal rosette at flowering. Compare flower stalks and the flower tube with similar centauries.
actions: Use close photographs of the whole plant and flowers to confirm it. Check regional status before removing a small pink-flowered plant from natural habitat.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust and Dutch botanical flora are distinct authorships. The two pages differ in botanical name-author citation; species concept and catalog ID retained.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: Native Europe/Asia/northern Africa; introduced North America; disturbed sites and fields.
Small annual without rosette, opposite leaves, branching flowering habit and stalked pink flowers.

proposedDescription: Branching bryozoan is a colony of tiny marine animals that builds a hard crust over rocks, shells and harbor structures. Older portions can become thick, dark brown or purplish, while growing edges are paler; some colonies develop folded sheets or hollow branches. Its animals collect suspended food with fine tentacles. Originally described from Naples, it is associated with warm coastal waters. Similar bryozoans have often been confused with it, so older reports from distant coastlines need careful checking.
identification: Look for a hard, layered crust with pale growing margins and darker older growth. Colony shape and color are insufficient for a firm identification; microscopic skeletal features need specialist examination.
actions: Photograph the colony and its location before seeking identification. Have attached growth assessed before moving marine equipment between waters.
researchNotes: Taxonomic caution: NEMESIS page 156301 now treats Schizoporella variabilis. San Francisco bryolith records formerly called S. errata were reassigned; none are presented here as S. errata ecology. DORIS broad worldwide range not repeated because revision documents extensive confusion.

sources.title: Tompsett, Porter & Taylor (2009), Taxonomy of Schizoporella unicornis and S. errata

claims: Type-based identity; layered or tubular colonies, pale tips and red-purple-brown older regions; historical misidentifications.
Shallow quiet-water hard substrates; dark colonies with paler edges; suspension feeding.
San Francisco colonies formerly identified as S. errata now S. variabilis; supports exclusion of those occurrence claims.

proposedDescription: Brazilian begonia is a small, soft-stemmed tropical plant with green leaves covered in fine hairs. It can flower while still only a few centimeters tall, producing small white blossoms above the foliage. Its papery brown fruits hold numerous dustlike seeds. The species is native to Jamaica and parts of tropical South America and favors moist tropical settings. It is also found outside that range; Singapore records it as a casual nonnative plant rather than assigning it a broad invasive status.
identification: Look for succulent stems, softly hairy green leaves, very pale hairy stipules and small white flowers. Use fruit and flower details to distinguish it from other small begonias.
actions: Confirm identification before removing a small begonia. Keep unwanted seedlings and seed-bearing potting material contained rather than discarding them into nearby vegetation.
researchNotes: Kew describes annual habit; NParks describes perennial lifespan in Singapore. Draft avoids forcing one lifespan across regions. Native range follows Kew; Singapore status is explicitly local.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Begonia hirtella

claims: Succulent herb, hairy leaves and stipules, white flowers, papery fruits, dustlike seeds, casual nonnative Singapore status.
Accepted species; native Jamaica and southern tropical America; wet tropical biome.

proposedDescription: Brazilian jasmine is a woody, evergreen climber with opposite leaves divided into three leaflets. Its white, tubular flowers open into narrow spreading lobes and have a noticeable fragrance. Despite its common name, the species comes from Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Introduced as an ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in southern Florida, where it can climb into forest canopies and cover other vegetation. Birds and mammals carry its seeds, helping it spread away from planted vines.
identification: Check for opposite leaves with three stalked leaflets, the middle leaflet usually larger, and clusters of white tubular flowers. Leaf hairiness varies and should not be used alone.
actions: In areas where it escapes, avoid planting it near natural vegetation. Photograph flowers and leaves for confirmation, and seek local advice before tackling large vines in tree canopies.
researchNotes: Flora of Somalia allows hairy or hairless leaves; UF account emphasizes pubescence. Draft uses shared reliable traits. Native range follows Kew rather than inferring Brazil from common name.

sources.title: UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Jasminum fluminense
Kew: Jasminum fluminense, including Flora of Somalia account

claims: Woody evergreen climber; trifoliolate leaves, fragrant white flowers; southern Florida forest invasion and animal seed dispersal.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: M. Thulin and Flora of Somalia authors / Kew taxonomy
claims: African-Arabian native range; three-leaflet opposite leaves, variable pubescence, tubular white flowers.

proposedDescription: Brazilian joyweed is a long-lived herb or small shrub often grown for its purple or reddish foliage. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, and small whitish flowers gather into rounded or slightly elongated heads on slender stalks. Shaded plants may be much greener than plants in sun. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has been planted elsewhere as an ornamental. Stems can root where they touch the ground, and discarded cuttings can help it spread beyond gardens.
identification: Look for paired leaves, young reddish or purplish hairy stems and small white flower heads on stalks. Leaf color varies with growing conditions and cultivated forms.
actions: Contain trimmings and rooted stem pieces. Check nearby ground for rooting branches before moving or disposing of an unwanted plant.
researchNotes: Kew provides native range. Brisbane provides species morphology; UF risk assessment quotes independent regional studies for vegetative spread. Cultivar-specific threat findings were not generalized.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Alternanthera brasiliana weed risk assessment

claims: Perennial herb/shrub; opposite leaves with variable green-purple color; stalked white flower clusters.
Accepted species native Mexico to tropical America.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: UF assessment quoting PIER and separate regional field reports
claims: Cultivation and spread through discarded cuttings or stems rooting at nodes.

proposedDescription: Brazilian nightshade is a sprawling perennial shrub or climber grown for loose clusters of mauve-blue, star-shaped flowers. Its leaves are deeply divided, and the flowers are followed by small, bright red berries. The stems lack prickles, a useful feature when comparing it with other nightshades. It has escaped ornamental plantings into moist sites in parts of Australia. In Florida, current guidance varies by region, with central and southern areas advised to manage plantings to prevent escape.
identification: Look for a prickless climber with deeply lobed leaves, clusters of mauve-blue flowers and red berries about a centimeter wide. Photograph flowers and fruit together for confirmation.
actions: Prevent garden vines from spreading into nearby vegetation. Seek local identification and control advice if a plant appears outside cultivation.
researchNotes: NSW and UF give differing native-range summaries, so no precise native boundary asserted. Regional Florida assessment is not generalized to all locations.

claims: Prickless perennial climber; divided leaves, mauve-blue flowers, red berries; naturalized moist NSW sites.
2026 central/south Florida caution to prevent escape; north Florida undocumented problem status.

proposedDescription: Brazilian Peppertree is an evergreen shrub or small tree with dense branches, glossy compound leaves and clusters of small red fruits. The leaves have several leaflets along a central stalk, which may be narrowly winged. Native to South America, it was widely planted as an ornamental and now forms dense thickets in parts of Florida and Hawaii. Birds help disperse its single-seeded fruits. It grows in many disturbed and natural habitats, including relatively dry ground within otherwise wet landscapes.
identification: Look for alternate compound leaves, usually five to nine leaflets, small pale flowers and dense clusters of red, peppercorn-sized fruits. Do not crush leaves to test their scent; sap can irritate skin.
actions: Avoid direct sap contact when handling it. In affected regions, seek local guidance for removal and follow-up because cut or damaged plants can sprout again.
researchNotes: Species-level account; retained separately from catalog variety row. UF and Forest Service overlap on some cited studies, but FEIS also draws on independent vegetation and habitat studies. Current feminine spelling retained.

sources.title: US Forest Service FEIS: Brazilian pepper

evidence.independentSourceGroup: UF CAIP / Barkley morphology and dispersal studies
claims: Evergreen shrub/tree, compound leaves, red single-seeded fruits, bird dispersal and contact irritation.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: USFS FEIS / independent regional vegetation studies
claims: Dense thickets, Florida/Hawaii habitats, growth on drier wetland microsites, root sprouting.

proposedDescription: Brazilian peppertree appears in this catalog under an older variety name. Kew now treats the corrected form, Schinus terebinthifolia var. raddiana, as a synonym of the typical variety. The broader species is an evergreen shrub or small tree with compound leaves and red fruits, but those features do not distinguish this historical variety. Keeping the naming history visible helps connect older records with current references without implying that this entry represents a separately identifiable plant.
identification: No variety-specific field characters were verified. Record the whole plant, compound leaves, flowers and fruits, and ask a botanical specialist to assess the name.
actions: Confirm the taxonomic meaning of any record using this variety name before assigning an identification or management recommendation.
researchNotes: RESEARCH GAP: Kew synonymizes var. raddiana with var. terebinthifolia; IPNI catalogs original var. raddianus nomenclature; Calflora marks name inactive and redirects to species. Two independent resources establish naming context, but no reliable variety-specific diagnostic account was verified. Species-level features are explicitly labeled; IDs not merged.

claims: Variety name is synonym of var. terebinthifolia.
Name inactive, associated with Brazilian peppertree tree/shrub.
Species-level evergreen tree/shrub, compound leaves and red fruit; not variety diagnostics.

proposedDescription: Brazilian vervain is a tall, rough-haired herb with branching stems and slender spikes of tiny bluish-purple flowers. Opposite, toothed leaves sit directly on the angular stems. Native to South America, it grows in fields, roadsides, damp grassland and stream margins where introduced, including North Carolina. It is easily confused with other tall verbenas. The small flower size and the bracts projecting among the flowers are more useful clues than its overall silhouette alone.
identification: Check angular, bristly stems, opposite toothed leaves and narrow flower spikes. Floral bracts are about as long as the calyx, unlike the generally shorter bracts of V. bonariensis.
actions: Have flowering material identified before removing tall verbenas, which include similar species. Where control is warranted, prevent mature seed from being moved with cut vegetation.
researchNotes: NC State and Flora Zambesiaca are separately authored morphology/ecology accounts. VicFlora search surfaced a putative hybrid treatment, but that page failed actual access; not used as verified evidence or silently substituted.

claims: South American origin, angular bristly stems, sessile leaves, small flowers, disturbed/wet habitats.
Damp grassland and stream habitats; flower-bract distinctions from V. bonariensis.

proposedDescription: Brazilian water hyacinth is an aquatic herb that holds its leaves and branching flower clusters above the water. Its broad leaves have heart-shaped bases and long, slender stalks that are not swollen. A study in northeastern Brazil described upright plants about 25–60 centimeters tall with many flowers in each cluster. Current botanical references place it in Pontederia as Pontederia paniculata. It is a separate species from the familiar floating water hyacinth, so that plant's growth habits and impacts should not be assumed here.
identification: Look for upright emergent growth, basal leaves with heart-shaped bases, unswollen leaf stalks and a many-flowered branching cluster. Seek a specialist determination when no flowers are present.
actions: Photograph leaves, stalks and flower clusters in place. Confirm identity and local status before removing or moving an aquatic plant.
researchNotes: Kew accepts Pontederia paniculata; catalog Eichhornia ID retained. Kew native range includes Florida, southern Mexico and tropical America, so no U.S.-wide nonnative claim. Flora species-specific emergent morphology used; no E. crassipes ecology transferred.

claims: Accepted current name; aquatic habit and native-range context.
Species account1.4: emergent upright herb,25-60cm; unswollen stalks, cordate leaf bases, many-flowered branching clusters.

proposedDescription: Brazilian Waterweed is a submerged freshwater plant with long, branching stems and dense rings of bright green leaves. Rooted near the bottom, it grows upward and often concentrates its foliage close to the surface. White flowers rise to the water surface during warmer months. Native to South America, it became familiar through ponds and aquariums. In invaded Washington waters, thick growth can crowd other aquatic plants, slow water movement and interfere with recreation.
identification: Look for leaves usually in rings of four or five, closely spaced near shoot tips, and conspicuous white three-petaled flowers. Related waterweeds require careful comparison of leaf size and arrangement.
actions: Do not release aquarium plants into waterways. Keep plant fragments off equipment being moved between waters, and report suspected new growth through local aquatic-weed channels.
researchNotes: Washington impacts remain regional. NSW account supplies independent morphology; species not confused with native Elodea. USGS access failed and is not cited.

sources.title: Washington Invasive Species Council: Brazilian elodea

claims: Dense whorled foliage, surface flowers, regional impacts and aquarium-release prevention.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: S.W.L. Jacobs / P.G. Kodela NSW Herbarium
claims: Submerged rooted perennial,4-5-leaf whorls, white flowers, still/slow waters, South American origin.

proposedDescription: Bridal bouquet is a vigorous climbing vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large sprays of tiny white flowers. The undersides of its leaves are covered in pale, silvery hairs, giving foliage a two-tone appearance. Native from the Indian subcontinent to Myanmar, it has been cultivated in other warm regions. Hawaiian specimens document vines spreading across fences, shrubs and trees, sometimes reaching well into the canopy. The small flowers may have a faint sweet fragrance.
identification: Look for alternate heart-shaped leaves with silvery hairy undersides and branched clusters of small white flowers. Compare the whole vine and flower details rather than relying on the common name.
actions: Keep cultivated vines from spreading onto nearby vegetation. Seek local advice for large plants in trees, and avoid moving unidentified vine material to new sites.
researchNotes: Bishop Museum combines botanical description with independent field specimen notes. Kew native-range synthesis is separate. No universal invasive claim; Hawaiian naturalization and growth records specified.

sources.title: Bishop Museum Plants of Hawai‘i: Poranopsis paniculata

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Bishop Museum flora and field collectors Staples/Lorence/Parker
claims: Heart-shaped silvery-underleaf vine, white flower sprays, naturalized Hawaiian growth over structures and vegetation.
Accepted liana native Indian subcontinent to Myanmar; introduced-range context.

proposedDescription: Bristly bellflower is a rough-haired wildflower with pale blue to lilac bells packed into rounded clusters. Its lower leaves are narrow, and the upright stem is thick and angular. Plants often begin as a leafy rosette before flowering in a later season. It grows around woodland edges, open woods and other partly open habitats in Europe. Its status deserves local attention: conservation work in Bavaria aims to support remaining populations, showing why a catalog listing alone cannot establish that a plant is unwanted.
identification: Look for coarse hairs, narrow lower leaves and dense clusters of pale blue-lilac bells at the stem tip and upper leaf axils. Photograph mature flowers for comparison with other clustered bellflowers.
actions: Confirm identity and regional conservation status before collecting or removing it. Record a suspected occurrence with photographs and a precise location.
researchNotes: French account calls plant perennial; Bavaria usually biennial. Draft avoids fixed global lifespan. Native-region conservation evidence prevents unsupported invasive labeling.

sources.title: Bavarian Environment Agency: Campanula cervicaria conservation
Conservatoire botanique de Lorraine: Campanula cervicaria

claims: Rosette then usually second-year flowering; open woods/edges; regional population support.
Rough hairs, thick angular stems, narrow basal leaves, clustered pale blue-lilac flowers, woodland ecology.

proposedDescription: Bristly dogstail grass is an annual grass with a dense, egg-shaped flower head covered in long, stiff bristles. Its narrow leaves are flat, and its upright stems may grow alone or in small tufts. Each head contains a mixture of fertile and sterile flower units, which contributes to its distinctive bristly outline. In British Columbia it occurs in disturbed ground, dry forest edges and thin-soiled Garry oak habitats, where managing seed production can help protect sensitive native vegetation.
identification: Look for a compact, bristly, oval head with paired fertile and fanlike sterile spikelets. Grass identification may require a close photograph or specimen checked by a botanist.
actions: Identify surrounding grasses before removal. Where local control is needed, pull small plants before seed set while minimizing disturbance to thin soils.
researchNotes: Retained catalog Cynosurus name; modern alternate genus Falona surfaced only in NCBI search and is not adopted without authoritative revision. Regional impacts limited to GOERT context.

sources.title: Garry Oak Ecosystems Recovery Team: Cynosurus echinatus
Flora of New Zealand: Cynosurus echinatus

claims: Bristly annual, paired fertile/sterile spikelets, dry disturbed habitats, seed persistence and careful early pulling.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Edgar and Connor Flora of New Zealand
claims: Annual tufted/solitary habit, flat leaves, compact oval bristly inflorescence.

proposedDescription: Bristly hawkbit is a dandelion-like herb whose leaves form a rosette close to the ground. Flower stalks rise above it with yellow flower heads, while the leaves vary from lightly toothed to deeply divided. Many plants carry forked or branching hairs, although hairiness varies among forms. A familiar grassland plant in parts of Europe and the Alps, it is also recorded as an introduced plant in New England fields, lawns and roadsides. Mature fruits help distinguish it from similar hawkbits.
identification: Examine the basal leaves and their branching hairs, then compare mature seed heads. The well-developed feathery fruit bristles across the head help separate it from L. saxatilis.
actions: Photograph the rosette, flower stalk and mature seed head for identification. Check local status before deciding whether a patch needs removal.
researchNotes: FAO treats L. hispidus sensu lato including glabrous subsp. hastilis; GoBotany New England account specifically subsp. hispidus. Draft acknowledges variation and does not merge taxon IDs.

sources.title: FAO: Site-specific grasses and herbs, Leontodon hispidus

claims: Basal leaves, branching hairs, fruit-bristle distinction, introduced New England disturbed habitats.
Rosette-forming perennial, variable leaf division/hairs, Alpine grassland/restoration context.

proposedDescription: Bristly Lady's Thumb is a low, often sprawling annual with slender spikes of tiny pink flowers. Its smooth stems bear alternate leaves, sometimes marked with a faint dark blotch. A papery sheath circles each leaf base, with conspicuously long bristles along its upper edge. Native to Asia, the species is introduced in much of eastern North America. At Fontenelle Forest in Nebraska it is common along trails, where its loose growth and small flower spikes can be easy to overlook.
identification: Check the long fringe on each papery stem sheath, alternate lance-shaped leaves and narrow pink flower spikes. A leaf blotch alone does not distinguish it from other smartweeds.
actions: Take close photographs of the stem sheaths and flowers before acting. Where an unwanted patch is confirmed, avoid carrying seed-bearing material to new locations.
researchNotes: Older references may use Polygonum cespitosum var. longisetum; Kew confirms this synonym. Do not equate all Persicaria cespitosa records with this species.

sources.title: Fontenelle Forest Nature Search: Bristly lady's thumb

claims: Sprawling annual, long-bristled sheaths, alternate leaves, pink spikes and Nebraska trail occurrence.
Asian native range, introduced North American distribution, synonymy and annual habit.

proposedDescription: Bristly oxtongue is a coarse herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and conspicuously rough leaves. Many of its hooked hairs arise from small raised bumps, giving the plant a prickly appearance. Beneath each flower head, several broad outer bracts surround a narrower inner set. It grows in fields, gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Native around the Mediterranean region, it has been introduced elsewhere, including North America, and older references often call it Picris echioides.
identification: Look for hooked bristles on raised leaf bumps and three to five broad outer bracts beneath each yellow head. These bracts help separate it from other yellow-flowered roadside herbs.
actions: Use gloves if handling the coarse foliage. Confirm the flower-head bracts before choosing a removal approach, especially among similar wildflowers.
researchNotes: Flora van Nederland describes biennial/sometimes longer-lived plants; lifespan omitted to accommodate variation. Picris echioides synonym noted.

sources.title: Kew: Helminthotheca echioides, Flora of Iraq

claims: Hooked tubercle-based hairs; field/garden/ditch habitats; Mediterranean range and introduced North America.
Yellow heads, broad outer and narrow inner bracts, rough foliage and synonym Picris echioides.

proposedDescription: Brittle Waternymph is a submerged freshwater plant with narrow, curved leaves and teeth visible along their edges. Leaves grow in pairs, though crowded shoots may look whorled. Its flowers and seeds are tiny and sit near the leaf bases. Native to parts of Europe, Africa and Asia, it has spread in North America through seeds and fragments. Some invaded waters develop dense growth, but effects vary: Wisconsin reports that nuisance-level growth has not been observed there.
identification: Look for recurved narrow leaves with obvious marginal teeth and no spines along the stem. Mature curved seeds and a botanical key help separate it from native naiads.
actions: Remove aquatic fragments from boats and equipment, drain retained water, and follow local drying guidance. Report suspected new occurrences before attempting large-scale removal.
researchNotes: Impacts explicitly variable and Wisconsin-specific absence of nuisance growth is attributed to DNR, not inferred. GoBotany key distinguishes target from native Najas.

claims: Paired curved toothed leaves, seeds/fragments dispersal, variable nuisance impacts and equipment hygiene.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Haines / Hellquist-Crow and Haynes botanical keys
claims: N. minor curved seed axis, recurved leaves and visible multicellular leaf teeth.

proposedDescription: Brittlestem hempnettle is an annual in the mint family with square, bristly stems and opposite, coarsely toothed leaves. Clusters of tubular pink, purple or white flowers sit where the upper leaves meet the stem. Each blossom has an arched upper lip and a spreading lower lip with darker markings near its base. Native from Europe to southwestern Siberia, it is introduced in North America, including British Columbia. Its nettle-like foliage can disguise its distinctive flowers until they open.
identification: Check square bristly stems, opposite stalked leaves and two-lipped flowers in tight leaf-axil clusters. The middle lower-lip lobe is unnotched, helping distinguish it from G. bifida.
actions: Use photographs of open flowers and stem nodes for confirmation. Avoid carrying mature seed-bearing plants between sites when removing a confirmed unwanted patch.
researchNotes: E-Flora documents hybrid evolutionary origin but accepted species status is retained; no inference that current individuals are casual hybrids. No medicinal or food advice.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Illustrated Flora of British Columbia authors
claims: Annual habit; bristly square stems, opposite toothed leaves, flower-lip characters; exotic BC status.
Accepted annual native Europe to SW Siberia; North American introduction.

proposedDescription: Broadleaf Dock is a sturdy perennial that starts as a rosette of large leaves with heart-shaped bases. Later it sends up a tall, ribbed flowering stem, with smaller leaves above and branching clusters of tiny greenish flowers. These clusters turn reddish brown as the fruits mature, and older foliage may also become reddish. A large fleshy taproot supports repeat growth. It is a familiar plant of disturbed ground and occurs along waterways in places such as Arizona.
identification: Look for broad lower leaves with heart-shaped bases and slightly wavy edges. Check the toothed, three-winged coverings around mature fruits; narrow, strongly curled leaves suggest a different dock.
actions: Confirm the mature fruit characters before removing docks. For an unwanted established plant, use local weed guidance that accounts for its persistent taproot.
researchNotes: Arizona calls it introduced and riparian; no precise global origin asserted. Arizona's alternate common name curly dock is not adopted because it risks confusion with R. crispus.

sources.title: University of Missouri WeedID: Broadleaf dock

claims: Taprooted perennial rosette, broad cordate leaves, ribbed stems and green-to-brown flowers/fruits.
Introduced perennial, riparian occurrence, broad heart-based leaves and reddish maturity.

proposedDescription: Broadleaf helleborine is a terrestrial orchid with an upright stem, broad leaves and a loose line of small flowers. Its leaves alternate up the stem, with parallel veins and lower bases that partly wrap around it. Flowers combine green, pink or purplish tones and have a shaped lower lip rather than a long spur. Native across much of Europe and Asia and parts of North Africa, it has become established in North America, sometimes appearing in disturbed garden or woodland settings.
identification: Look for alternate parallel-veined leaves and small orchid flowers with a constricted, pointed lower lip. Confirm flowering plants with an orchid specialist before disturbing them.
actions: Photograph the flowers and leaves in place. Check local identity and status before removal because native orchids can occur nearby.
researchNotes: Species account, not entire E. helleborine aggregate. Kew recognizes several infraspecific taxa; draft does not assert their traits or status. Maryland advice used only for disturbed habitat context and cautious local review.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Orchid in my garden

claims: Perennial upright orchid; alternate sheathing leaves and green-pink flowers with unspurred lip.
Native NW Africa/Europe-China; introduced North America; rhizomatous habit.
Disturbed habitat occurrence and need to distinguish local native orchids.

proposedDescription: Broadleaf rush is a tufted perennial that can look like a small clump of grass until its branched flower clusters develop. Flat leaves gather at the base, while the stems carry an open, umbrella-like arrangement of small rounded flower heads. Brown capsules follow the flowers. It favors open, damp ground, including exposed clay and track or drain margins. Native in parts of the Southern Hemisphere, including New Zealand and Australia, it is introduced in places such as Hawaii and Oregon.
identification: Check flat basal leaves and an open, branched cluster of rounded flower heads. Similar woodrushes usually have conspicuous hairs along their leaf margins; this rush lacks that fringe.
actions: Photograph flowers or capsules as well as the leaf bases before identifying a grasslike wetland plant. Check regional status before disturbing a patch.
researchNotes: NZPCN and NZFlora share some source lineage, so Kew/Kirschner-Stace treatment supplies independent taxonomy/distribution. Australojuncus planifolius is a published alternative combination; Kew currently retains Juncus.

sources.title: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Juncus planifolius

claims: Flat basal leaves, branched heads, brown capsules, damp open-ground habitats and woodrush distinction.
Native southern Australia/New Zealand/Chile; introduced Hawaii/Oregon; alternate Australojuncus combination.

proposedDescription: Broadleaved pepperweed is a tall perennial in the mustard family, with smooth green to gray-green leaves and dense sprays of tiny white flowers. New shoots begin as low rosettes before sending up stiff stems. Underground, an extensive root system stores energy and produces more shoots. Introduced from southeastern Europe and Asia, it forms persistent stands in parts of the western United States, especially around waterways, wetlands and irrigated ground. Seeds and root pieces can move it into new areas.
identification: Look for many upright stems, smooth foliage, broad basal leaves and dense white flower clusters. Compare leaf attachment carefully with the shorter, clasping-leaved hoary cress.
actions: Prevent movement of contaminated soil and root pieces. Small seedlings may be pulled, but established patches need a sustained local management plan and follow-up for regrowth.
researchNotes: Sources share the UC system but have distinct authorship: R.G. Wilson extension synthesis versus UCSB riparian research group with field observations. Regional impact not global.

sources.title: UCSB Riparian InVasion Research Laboratory: Perennial pepperweed

claims: Morphology, European-Asian origin, root reserves and fragments, prevention and repeated-control needs.
Western North American riparian abundance and movement along drainage canals into fields.

proposedDescription: Brome fescue is a small annual grass with slender stems, narrow leaves and a compact, bristly flower cluster held clear of the uppermost leaf sheath. Its spikelets contain several flowers, each with a fine projecting awn. It grows in a wide range of open habitats, from coastal ground to dry inland sites, and is introduced from Europe in Washington. Some current references call it Festuca bromoides, while regional floras continue to use the catalog name Vulpia bromoides.
identification: Look for an exposed narrow flower cluster and compare the two unequal glumes at each spikelet base. A close-up of mature spikelets is more useful than a distant grass photograph.
actions: Confirm the species before removing annual grasses from mixed vegetation. Avoid moving ripe seed heads with soil or equipment from an unwanted patch.
researchNotes: Kew accepts Festuca bromoides; Burke retains Vulpia. Catalog ID preserved with explicit alternative name. No blanket invasive status inferred from introduced occurrence.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Don Knoke / David Giblin and regional flora
claims: Annual habit, narrow leaves, exposed awned panicle; broad habitat range and European introduction.
Vulpia bromoides synonym of Festuca bromoides.

proposedDescription: Bronze bug is a tiny, flattened brown insect that lives on eucalyptus foliage. Adults and orange young insects may gather on the same leaves, alongside clusters of black eggs. Feeding can turn leaves reddish, then yellow-brown, giving affected crowns their bronze appearance; heavy infestations may thin the canopy. Native to Australia, it has spread to eucalyptus plantings in several other regions. Its small size and similarity to related bugs make a close examination more dependable than leaf discoloration alone.
identification: Look for flattened, light-brown adults, orange nymphs with dark markings, and clustered black eggs on eucalyptus leaves. Confirm suspected specimens with a specialist.
actions: Photograph insects and damage, keep infested foliage from being moved to new sites, and seek local forestry or plant-health advice before treatment.
researchNotes: FAO's dated distribution is used for origin and biology, not as a current complete range. Independent Novoselsky and Freidberg field survey confirms eucalyptus association in Israel; only its explicit abstract was accessed. No phloem-specific feeding claim.

sources.title: FAO: Bronze bug forest pest profile
Novoselsky and Freidberg: First record in the Middle East

claims: Australian origin; adult and immature appearance; egg clusters; leaf discoloration and canopy thinning; movement on infested plant material.
Observed on Eucalyptus camaldulensis in Israel in 2014; eucalyptus host association and identification study.

proposedDescription: Odontites vulgaris, usually called red bartsia, is a downy annual of open grassland. Slender, branching stems carry narrow, toothed leaves and small pink flowers with two lips. Plants can reach about half a metre tall. They make their own green growth while also drawing resources from grass roots, a habit called partial parasitism. Native in Britain and Ireland, red bartsia also appears in Canadian floristic records. The catalog's name 'broomrape' should not obscure its leafy, green appearance.
identification: Look for hairy, branched stems, narrow toothed leaves and small pink, two-lipped flowers. Confirm against local Odontites keys before assigning the species.
actions: Photograph flowering plants and their habitat, and confirm local status before removal. Keep seed-bearing material contained if local guidance calls for control.
researchNotes: Common-name review: catalog Broomrape is broader and potentially misleading; RHS and VASCAN use red bartsia. VASCAN accepts O. vulgaris under FNA 2019 and lists O. vernus misapplications separately. Canadian occurrence is stated without inferring status from map colors unavailable in text.

claims: Annual, downy stems to 50 cm, narrow toothed leaves, pink two-lipped flowers, grassland and partial grass-root parasitism; native GB/Ireland.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: VASCAN Canadian floristic synthesis and FNA taxonomy
claims: Accepted species, red bartsia common name, synonyms and Canadian provincial records.

proposedDescription: Brown anoles are small, quick-moving lizards often seen basking on low fences, tree trunks and sunny garden edges. Their brown or gray bodies commonly show pale stripes, spots or diamonds, and males display an orange-red throat fan with a pale border. They hunt insects and other small animals, usually close to the ground. Native to Caribbean islands, they are widespread introductions in Florida. Native green anoles can also turn brown, so body color alone is not a reliable identification.
identification: Look for a relatively short snout, bold back markings and, in displaying males, an orange-red throat fan with a pale border. Green anoles have longer snouts and can themselves be brown.
actions: Inspect potted plants, boats and stored equipment before moving them. Photograph unusual new sightings for local reporting, and retain varied vegetation and trees that provide habitat for native wildlife.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS and SREL are separately authored institutional accounts. Egg-laying intervals differ, so no fixed interval used. Florida impact is not generalized to the native range; no claim of inevitable green-anole extinction.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Georgia Savannah River Ecology Laboratory herpetology
claims: Size and coloration, shorter snout, ground and low-vegetation use, daylight activity and invertebrate diet.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: UF/IFAS Invasion Ecology authors and Steve Johnson
claims: Caribbean native range; Florida introduction; identification distinctions; transport in plants and boats; habitat support and reporting.

proposedDescription: Brown bryozoan forms branching, purplish-brown tufts that may look like miniature seaweed bushes. Each tuft is a colony of tiny animals that draw food particles from seawater. Colonies attach to rocks, pilings, floats, hulls and other submerged surfaces, sometimes becoming part of heavy marine fouling. The name Bugula neritina covers several genetically distinct forms with very similar appearances. Some have spread widely through human transport, while the origins and status of particular populations require closer investigation.
identification: Look for upright brown-to-purple branching tufts, with tiny beadlike brood chambers along branches. Microscopy supports identification of the complex; genetic work may be needed to distinguish its constituent species.
actions: Photograph colonies in place and seek marine-specialist confirmation. Inspect and clean fouled vessels and equipment using local biosecurity procedures before moving between waters.
researchNotes: Explicit species-complex treatment. SERC morphology/ecology draws on independently authored taxonomic literature including Osburn, Maturo and Ryland; Fehlauer-Ale et al. supplies primary genetic delimitation evidence. Do not infer all lineages are introduced everywhere. Primary paper accessed as institutional abstract.

sources.title: Fehlauer-Ale et al.: Cryptic species in the Bugula neritina complex

evidence.independentSourceGroup: SERC NEMESIS morphology/ecology synthesis of Osburn, Maturo and Ryland
claims: Purplish bushy colonies, brood chambers, suspension feeding, hard substrates and hull fouling; variable population origins.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Fehlauer-Ale, Mackie, Lim-Fong, Ale, Pie and Waeschenbach genetic study

proposedDescription: Brown flatsedge is a small annual sedge that forms tufts on damp, open ground beside ponds, streams and ditches. Smooth stems and narrow leaves support clusters of flattened flower spikes, often dark reddish-brown but sometimes yellow-green. It takes advantage of muddy or sandy margins exposed as water levels fall. The species is native across much of Europe and parts of Africa and Asia, with introduced records in North America. Its local status matters: in Germany, it is a native conservation concern.
identification: Look for small tufts, smooth stems, narrow leaves and branching clusters of short, flattened dark spikelets. Mature fruit and flower scales help distinguish similar sedges.
actions: Photograph mature heads and the wetland setting; seek botanical confirmation before removal. Check local conservation and nonnative status, and avoid moving mud or seed-bearing material between wetlands.
researchNotes: FloraWeb directly supports morphology, seasonally exposed shores and German native/threatened status; Kew independently provides global range and North American introductions. Failed Israeli/FNA/BSBI fetches were not counted.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Cyperus fuscus

evidence.independentSourceGroup: German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation FloraWeb
claims: Small annual tufts; smooth stems; narrow leaves; dark or yellow-green spikelets; seasonally exposed wet shores; native and threatened in Germany.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew taxonomic backbone
claims: Accepted annual species; native Macaronesia, Europe, Mediterranean to China; introduced North American regions.

proposedDescription: Brown garden snail carries a rounded, coiled shell patterned with brown bands and pale flecks. Adults are often about three centimetres across, although size and markings vary. Most feeding happens at night or in damp weather, when snails leave shelter to rasp leaves, flowers and soft fruit. Silvery trails can reveal visits after the animals have hidden again. Long transported with plants and for food, this European snail became a troublesome garden and crop pest in California after its nineteenth-century introduction.
identification: Look for a globular, finely wrinkled shell with irregular brown spiral bands and pale flecks; mature shells have a turned-back opening lip. Confirm against local snails.
actions: Inspect plants and containers before transport. In affected gardens, reduce unnecessary damp shelter, irrigate early and hand-pick confirmed pest snails with gloves; check local disposal advice.
researchNotes: Cornu aspersum is the current name; Helix aspersa and Cantareus aspersus occur in older material. UF morphology derives from Burch and Capinera; UC IPM supplies independently authored garden management. No claim of establishment everywhere, particularly Florida.

sources.title: Dekle and Fasulo: Brown Garden Snail

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Dekle and Fasulo UF/FDACS account using Burch and Capinera morphology

evidence.independentSourceGroup: UC Statewide IPM garden pest authors
claims: Brown garden snail is a California garden pest; slime trails, moisture and shelter; irrigation and hand-picking management.

proposedDescription: Brown hoplo is a dark, armored catfish with two rows of hard plates along each side and two pairs of long whiskerlike barbels. It searches muddy bottoms for small invertebrates and decaying material in slow rivers, ponds, marshes and canals. Gulping air helps it cope with oxygen-poor water. Males make floating bubble nests mixed with vegetation and defend them during breeding. Native to South America, it has established in Florida, where its unusual nests have been documented in shallow lake marshes.
identification: Look for a dark brown-to-black catfish with paired rows of body armor and two pairs of long chin barbels. Breeding males have enlarged pectoral spines.
actions: Photograph unfamiliar catches and report suspected new occurrences to local fisheries staff. Do not transfer live fish between water bodies, and obtain current local guidance before keeping or releasing a catch.
researchNotes: FWC species account paired with Nico and Muench's independently authored field study of 22 nests. ResearchGate author-posted full article was readable. USGS NAS direct fetch failed and is not cited. No unsupported whole-ecosystem impact or exact introduction pathway claimed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Nico and Muench 2004 primary field observations

proposedDescription: Brown marmorated stink bugs are broad, shield-shaped insects with mottled brown bodies and pale bands on their antennae. Adults are roughly the size of a fingernail. They feed on many fruits, vegetables and ornamental plants, and their feeding can leave fruit distorted or damaged. Native to eastern Asia, they have become important crop pests in parts of North America. In autumn, adults often gather on buildings while looking for winter shelter; finding them indoors does not mean they are breeding in the house.
identification: Check for alternating pale and dark antennal bands and banding along the exposed abdomen edges. Several native stink bugs are brown, so shape and color alone are insufficient.
actions: Seal gaps and repair screens before autumn entry. For crop damage, confirm the insect and ask local extension staff about monitoring and appropriate management.
researchNotes: Penn State-authored PDF hosted by Texas A&M is counted as Penn State, not a separate Texas author. Maryland's local horticultural account supplies independent identification and host evidence. Old distribution counts and generation estimates omitted.

proposedDescription: Brown mustard is a leafy mustard crop grown for pungent greens and seeds used in condiments and oil. Plants usually grow as annuals, producing clusters of yellow, four-petaled flowers followed by slender seed pods that split when dry. Leaves vary greatly among cultivated forms, from green to purple and from relatively smooth to deeply lobed. It grows best in cool weather with adequate moisture. Widely introduced beyond its Eurasian origins, it can also occur as a weed, so cultivated plants and wild escapes need different context.
identification: Look for alternate leaves, yellow flowers with four petals and long pods containing round seeds. Cultivar leaf shape varies; flowers and mature pods help distinguish other mustards.
actions: Keep cultivated plants from scattering unwanted seed, and confirm escaped plants before removal. Check local weed guidance rather than assuming every mustard planting is invasive.
researchNotes: Taxonomy review: current Kew treats Brassica × juncea as synonym of × Brassarda juncea, reflecting hybrid origin; NC State retains Brassica juncea. Catalog ID retained. Kew limits native range to Caucasus; NC State gives broader Eurasian origin. No exact native boundary or vague state legal claims reproduced.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: × Brassarda juncea

claims: Annual crop; cool-season growth; yellow four-petaled flowers; split pods; variable leaf morphology; greens, condiment and oil uses.

claims: Accepted hybrid name, Brassica × juncea synonym, Caucasian native range and widespread introductions.

proposedDescription: Brown powderpost beetle is a small, flattened reddish-brown beetle associated with hardwood timber and wooden objects. Its cream-colored larvae tunnel through starch-rich sapwood, sometimes reducing the interior to very fine, flourlike powder. Round exit holes appear when adults emerge, making damage easier to notice than the insects themselves. Infested wood can carry the beetle between countries. The amount of damage depends on the wood and its sapwood content; powder and holes deserve identification before assumptions are made about structural danger.
identification: Look for slender brown adults with a visible head and clubbed antennae, fine powder and small round holes in hardwood. Retain a specimen for species confirmation.
actions: Inspect and set aside suspect wooden items, record fresh powder or emerging beetles, and consult a qualified wood-pest or conservation specialist before treatment.
researchNotes: Independent museum accounts differ in emphasis: NHM describes largely decorative damage in heartwood-dominated structural timber; Australian Museum notes serious weakening in susceptible wood. Draft avoids either absolute. Queensland powderpost page now names L. africanus and was excluded. No unsupported native continent.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: Lyctus brunneus identification

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Natural History Museum London identification authors
claims: Flattened brown adult, clubbed antennae, cream larvae, starch-rich hardwood sapwood, fine powder, exit holes and imported timber.
Species-specific hardwood egg laying and larval starch feeding, adult emergence holes, susceptibility-related timber damage and introduction in Australia.

proposedDescription: Lecanosticta acicola is a fungus that causes brown spot needle blight in pines. Small discolored spots can expand into brown bands, and infected needles may die at the tips or fall early, leaving a thin-looking crown. Wet needles and humid weather favor infection, while rain and wind spread spores. In New England, eastern white pine is a frequent host, though other pines are susceptible. Similar symptoms can come from other needle diseases, so the pattern of damage alone does not confirm this fungus.
identification: Look for brown needle spots or bands, sometimes with yellow margins, dying tips and early shedding. A plant diagnostic laboratory should distinguish it from Dothistroma and other needle pathogens.
actions: Ask a diagnostic service how to submit suspect needles before moving material. For confirmed disease, discuss airflow, tree spacing and suitable care with a local arborist or forestry adviser.
researchNotes: UMass Nicholas Brazee independently documents diagnostic submissions and New England disease ecology; Scion diagnostics uses EPPO morphology and transport evidence. Former name Mycosphaerella dearnessii noted. UMass regards it as North American native: not labeled universally nonnative. Scion 2023 New Zealand absence claim not repeated as current.

sources.title: UMass Extension: Brown Spot Needle Blight
Scion: Brown spot needle blight factsheet

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Nicholas Brazee UMass diagnostic and regional pathology account
claims: Lecanosticta acicola synonym; eastern white pine hosts; needle loss, wet-weather infection, spore dispersal and airflow management.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Scion forest-health diagnostics and EPPO diagnostic standard
claims: Needle spots, brown bands and yellow halos; similar Dothistroma symptoms; infected plant movement and laboratory identification.

proposedDescription: Brown spot of soybean is a leaf disease caused by the fungus Septoria glycines. Small brown patches usually appear low on the plant, often surrounded by yellowing tissue. The patches can merge and affected leaves may fall early. Warm, wet weather helps the disease develop, while infected crop remains can carry the fungus into the next season. Brown spot is common in soybean fields and often has little effect on yield; more serious damage is possible when it moves into the upper canopy.
identification: Look for irregular brown spots and yellowing that begin on lower soybean leaves. Several diseases look similar, so symptoms alone may not confirm the fungus.
actions: Ask a crop diagnostic service to confirm the cause before treatment. Use local extension guidance when deciding whether management is warranted.
researchNotes: Independent NC State and Cornell extension accounts agree on symptoms and variable severity. No national invasive-status claim or automatic fungicide recommendation.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Brown spot of soybean

claims: Pathogen, lower-canopy symptoms, wet-weather development and survival in debris
Common disease, symptoms and generally rare severe epidemics in NY

proposedDescription: Brown trout are introduced freshwater fish familiar to many anglers. Stream fish often have a golden-brown body with dark and reddish spots, while fish living in large lakes can look much more silvery. They eat aquatic insects and other small animals, including fish as they grow. Brought to the United States for fishing, they now live in many rivers and lakes. Their role depends on the waterway: some populations support managed fisheries, while others compete with native trout that conservation programs are working to protect.
identification: Compare the body spots, relatively square tail and head with a regional trout guide; lake fish may show less obvious spotting.
actions: Follow the rules for the specific waterbody, including any release requirements. Never move live fish between waters.
researchNotes: Michigan DNR supports morphology and managed fisheries; NPS documents introduced populations and competition with native trout. USGS page failed direct access and is not needed as supporting evidence.

sources.title: National Park Service: Yellowstone fish ecology

Brown trout introduction and competition with native cutthroat trout

proposedDescription: Brown widow spiders often make their webs in sheltered places around buildings, plant pots and outdoor furniture. Many are mottled tan or brown with an orange hourglass beneath the abdomen, but their colors vary enough to make identification tricky. Young black widows can look similar. A round egg sac covered in little silk spikes is a particularly useful clue. This nonnative spider is established in parts of the southern United States and Southern California. It can bite if pressed against the skin, so identification is best done without handling it.
identification: Photograph the spider and any spiky egg sacs from a safe distance. Color and an hourglass mark alone do not reliably separate it from other widows.
actions: Avoid handling spiders or reaching blindly into sheltered spaces. Reduce clutter around occupied areas and seek identification advice if unsure.
researchNotes: UCR's direct photographic comparison supports identification; UF Sarasota provides independently authored local habitat and prevention guidance. Shared egg-sac link does not count as independent evidence for that feature. Omitted sensational venom-potency comparisons.

sources.title: UC Riverside: How to identify brown widow spiders

claims: Variable coloration, spiky egg sacs, black-widow confusion and introduced distribution
Protected sites around structures, accidental-contact bite risk and sanitation

proposedDescription: The brown-dotted clothes moth is a small, easily overlooked moth with mottled brown wings and a tufted head. Its larvae feed on dry plant and animal material, often in bird nests or poultry houses where feathers and other remains collect. Despite its name, it is only occasionally associated with damage to clothing. Stored animal specimens can also provide food. Adults resemble other small nest moths, so finding one indoors does not by itself show that fabrics are being damaged.
identification: Look for small, mottled brown forewings with dark spots and a hairy head. Similar Niditinea species may require specialist confirmation.
actions: If moths recur indoors, seek identification and inspect nearby stored organic material for larvae or damage before choosing a treatment.
researchNotes: MuseumPests gives collection-specific biology; Dutch Microvlinders provides independent diagnostic comparison and explicitly requires confirmation for look-alikes. Avoided importing British flight months to US.

claims: Adult morphology, nest-associated larval diet and occasional collection/fabric damage
Small mottled adult with dark spots and similar N. striolella requiring confirmation

proposedDescription: Browne's blechum is a low herb with paired leaves and upright flower spikes. The overlapping green bracts around those spikes are often more noticeable than the tiny pale flowers, giving the plant its other name, green shrimp plant. Its stems can spread along the ground and root where they touch the soil. Native to tropical parts of the Americas, it has become established beyond that range and is listed as invasive in Florida. The square-looking flower spikes are a useful starting point for recognizing it.
identification: Photograph the paired, oval leaves and dense spikes of overlapping leafy bracts, including any small pale flowers.
actions: Check local invasive-plant guidance before moving it. If removing a confirmed plant by hand, include rooted stem sections to reduce regrowth.
researchNotes: Florida FLIP uses FNAI for morphology; independent Flora of China treatment read in complete cached morphological section via WFO because direct WFO fetch failed. Seed counts conflict between sources and are omitted.

proposedDescription: Brown knapweed is a perennial wildflower with purple-pink flower heads on upright, branching stems. Beneath each head are overlapping bracts with broad, brown, papery tips that look unevenly torn. Native to Europe, it has become established in North America in fields, meadows and disturbed ground, and can form large patches. It also crosses with black knapweed, producing plants that blur the usual identification clues. A close look at the bracts is more useful than flower color alone.
identification: Photograph the side and underside of a flower head to show its broad, irregularly torn brown bract tips; hybrids can be difficult to name.
actions: Seek local identification help before management, and check your state's knapweed guidance before moving plants or seed.
researchNotes: Independent Flora Novae Angliae and Illustrated Flora of BC support diagnosis. Omitted inconsistent seed-pappus and toxicity statements from other extension summaries; neither nationwide legal status nor blanket harmfulness inferred.

Perennial habit, purple flowers and broad papery tattered bract tips

proposedDescription: Browntail moths have white wings and a tuft of brown hair at the tip of the abdomen. Their caterpillars feed on trees and shrubs, including oaks, apples and cherries, and spend winter together in silk nests that hold dead leaves on branch tips. Established in parts of New England after introduction from Europe, they can strip foliage during outbreaks. The caterpillars' tiny hairs are also an important concern: they can irritate skin and breathing, even when carried on wind or left on surfaces.
identification: Look from a distance for dark, hairy caterpillars with white side markings and two red spots near the rear, or compact winter webs at branch tips.
actions: Avoid touching caterpillars or nests. Consult local forestry guidance for safe management and reporting; avoid disturbing infested material in ways that send hairs into the air.
researchNotes: Independent RHS identification/lifecycle corroborates Maine forestry guidance; British native status and UK management advice not transferred to US. Historical USDA leaflet used only for origin, not current range.

Adult/caterpillar morphology and winter nests

proposedDescription: Watersipora arcuata is a marine animal that grows in colonies, often as dark crusts with reddish growing edges. A colony is made up of many tiny connected individuals and can develop overlapping, curled layers. It attaches to hard surfaces such as rocks, docks and boat hulls, which can carry it between harbors. Records from Southern California and Hawaii reflect its history of introductions, although its original native range remains uncertain. Similar Watersipora species are hard to separate without examining their tiny skeletal features.
identification: Color and crust-like growth can suggest Watersipora, but a specialist needs microscopic features to confirm W. arcuata.
actions: Photograph suspected colonies and their location. Follow marina and local biofouling guidance; avoid moving fouled equipment or scraping organisms into another waterbody.
researchNotes: NEMESIS synthesis supports colony form, uncertain origin and hull transport; independently checked Reverter-Gil/Souto original examination of Spanish specimens in cached taxonomic section. Direct PMC blocked by browser check. Avoided conflicting older aperture descriptions and broad impacts.

proposedDescription: Buckhorn plantain grows as a clump of narrow, strongly ribbed leaves close to the ground. Slender, leafless stalks rise above them, ending in short flower heads ringed with pale, projecting stamens. Originally from Eurasia, it is now a familiar plant in lawns, paths, fields and other disturbed places across much of North America. Its low-growing leaves help it persist under mowing. Compared with broadleaf plantain, the leaves are much narrower and the flowering heads are usually shorter and more compact.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of narrow leaves with prominent lengthwise ribs and leafless stalks carrying compact flower heads.
actions: Where removal is needed, remove the crown as well as the leaves before seed develops; mowing alone often leaves the plant alive.
researchNotes: UC IPM weed morphology and management cross-checked against independent Flora Novae Angliae. No medicinal-use recommendation or assumption that every lawn plant requires eradication.

proposedDescription: Buckthorn aphids are tiny, soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap. They are usually pale yellow or green, and colonies can gather on the undersides of potato leaves. In colder regions they spend winter as eggs on buckthorn, then move to other plants during the growing season. Their importance in crops is not just the sap they take: they can carry potato viruses between plants. Several aphids look alike, making a careful identification useful before deciding how to respond.
identification: Adults are roughly 1–2 mm long, pale yellow to green, with short antennae and short rear tubes. Winged forms have a darker head and thorax.
actions: If found on a crop, ask local extension or a diagnostic service to identify it and advise on virus risk and monitoring.
researchNotes: Independent New Brunswick crop guidance and INRAE morphology/lifecycle agree. INRAE full short article read in search cache after direct timeout. Direct feeding severity differs regionally, so no universal yield-loss claim or numerical treatment threshold.
